blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A log-indexing job runs on a ForkJoinPool(6) and splits 600,000 lines by count into 24 leaves. The lines of one noisy service, 3% of the file and all together, take 100 times as long as the rest. The job takes almost as long as on one thread. What would change that?

options.text: Splitting into many more leaves, since a leaf that has started stays on one worker and the noisy lines now fill about one leaf
options.says: a thief takes only queued tasks, so the leaf that holds the expensive rows sets the time; smaller leaves spread those rows over many of them

options.text: Splitting into fewer, larger leaves, since 24 leaves is already four per worker and every extra leaf adds a task's overhead
options.says: four per worker left the options of the page's run in two leaves (567 ms against 163 ms); the leaf count has to follow where the cost is

options.text: Giving the pool more workers, since more workers can each take a share of the noisy leaf's lines while it runs
options.says: nothing takes part of a running leaf; extra workers only find more idle time

options.text: Giving the pool more time, since work-stealing moves the rest of a long leaf's lines to idle workers as the run goes on
options.says: work-stealing moves queued tasks, not part of a loop that is running

origin.section: Uneven Work Needs Many More Leaves Than Workers

questions.stem: A thumbnail task splits by cost: a batch whose pixels fit the budget is compressed by one task, and a bigger batch is cut where half its pixels are done, with the cut kept inside the batch. Its leaf test is only `pixels(from, to) <= budget`. One upload is a single scan larger than the budget. What happens to it?

options.text: The scan is compressed by one task, since a batch over the budget is cut until each part is within it or holds one file
options.says: only a leaf test that also accepts a single item stops there; with the budget test alone the one-file batch is cut again

options.text: The scan is compressed by two tasks, since a cut at half the pixels gives each half of the image to a different task
options.says: the cut is between items; a batch of one item can't be divided

options.text: The job never gets past the scan, since a batch of one file can't be cut and one of its halves is the whole batch again
options.says: a range of one item can't split, so it must be a leaf; otherwise one half is the whole range again and the task forks itself until the stack overflows

options.text: The job gets past the scan more slowly, since a batch that can't be cut by pixels is cut at the middle index instead
options.says: the task has no fallback to an index cut; the one-file batch splits into itself and an empty half

origin.section: When You Know What Each Item Costs, Split by Cost

questions.stem: A crawler's task holds 30 million URLs. It forks a task for the first 500 URLs, then calls compute() on a task for the rest, which does the same. On a test list of 20,000 URLs it was quick. What does it do on the full list?

options.text: It runs about as fast as halving would, since other workers steal each 500-URL task as soon as it is forked
options.says: the steals do happen, but compute() on the rest is a call on the same thread, one stack frame per chunk: about 60,000 frames, far past the 7,999 that overflowed on the page's run

options.text: It runs on one worker only, since a forked 500-URL task waits until the rest of the list has been computed
options.says: forked chunks are queued and other workers steal them at once; the test run was fast

options.text: It fails with a StackOverflowError, since every chunk adds one more nested call on the stack of a single thread
options.says: peeling adds a frame per chunk; 7,999 chunks overflowed a worker's stack on the page's run, while halving went 13 levels deep

options.text: It fails with a RejectedExecutionException, since every chunk adds one more task to a queue that has a fixed size
options.says: the page's peel failed on the stack, not on a queue; the forked chunks were stolen as they came

origin.section: The Split Point Sets the Depth: Halve, or Fork the Chunks From a Loop

questions.stem: A reviewer flags a task that cuts each range 20/80 instead of in half, over rows that all cost the same, with the same threshold. Compared with halving, what does the 20/80 cut change?

options.text: Fewer tasks and a shallower tree, since the larger part reaches the threshold in fewer cuts than a half does
options.says: the larger part shrinks more slowly than a half, so the tree gets deeper; the page's 10/90 made 48,531 tasks against 16,383

options.text: A slower job overall, since the worker that keeps the 80% part does most of the work while the others wait
options.says: the page's 10/90 was no slower than 50/50 (47 ms against 53): on even work an uneven ratio costs tasks, and the time doesn't show it

options.text: More tasks and a deeper tree, since the larger part needs more cuts than a half before it reaches the threshold
options.says: the 10/90 run went 86 levels deep with three times the tasks and the same time: on even work an uneven ratio wastes tasks, not balance

options.text: The same tasks and the same depth, since the threshold alone decides how many leaves a range of that many rows ends up in
options.says: the split ratio changes the tree: the page's 10/90 made 48,531 tasks 86 levels deep, against 16,383 and 13 for 50/50, at the same threshold

origin.section: The Split Point Sets the Depth: Halve, or Fork the Chunks From a Loop

concepts: Forking one chunk and computing the rest recursively adds a stack frame per chunk and overflows on large inputs; halving adds a level per halving.
Work-stealing moves only queued tasks; neither stealing nor more workers shares a leaf that has started.
On even work an uneven split ratio makes a deeper tree and more tasks but no slower a job.
